Let \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) additionally satisfy \(\texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}\).  Because the event \(\{X_1=e\}\) is observable, every \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\) also assigns it probability zero in each cohort.  For each \(d\) and \(j\), nonnegativity gives
\[
 0=P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=\sum_{j=1}^2P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d),
\]
so each summand is zero.  Hence
\[
 \pi_j^d=P(Z=j\mid D=d)
 =P(Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A\mid D=d)=\alpha_j^d.               \tag{1}
\]
The broad recovery theorem \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) identifies the entire component sublaw on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\); under the present restriction that event has conditional probability one, so this is the full component law of \((Z,X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)\).  In particular,
\[
 P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=d,Z=j)
 =(\pi_j^d)^{-1}s_j^dQ_j.                                   \tag{2}
\]
By the same causal conditioning used in that theorem,
\[
 \tau_j
 =P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=1,Z=j)(R_j^1-R_j^0)
 =\frac{\nu_j}{\pi_j^1}=\eta_j.                            \tag{3}
\]
Equations (1)--(3) recover \(\pi_j^d\), the full conditional component laws, \(\tau_j\), and \(\tau=\sum_j\pi_j^1\tau_j=\sum_j\nu_j\), in the common descending signature order, throughout the full compatible fiber.  They also prove \(\Phi(p)=\theta\) for the contribution-and-aggregate target.  Since the broad theorem did not use date \(4\) or time homogeneity, neither does this corollary.  At the absorbing cut the common exit row remains \((0,0,1)\), so the all-state terminal factor is singular and strict positivity fails even though the four active minors suffice.

Let \(q_d(p)=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}p_s\).  Cohort overlap gives \(q_d(p)>0\).  Every cohort-conditional entry in \(A_{xy}^d\) and \(m_x^d\) is a linear marginal of the \(126\)-cell vector divided by \(q_d(p)\).  The proof of \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) shows that, at every compatible regular \(p\), all slice determinants, \(\det(B_a^d)\), \(\det(W^d)\), \(\det(B_b^d)\), row-sum normalizers, active masses, and determinants \(\det\{C_y^d(C_y^d)^\top\}\) used in a division are nonzero, while \((g^d)^2>0\).

Let \(\mathcal U_p\) be the subset of the affine hyperplane \(\{z:\mathbf 1^\top z=1\}\) on which the same finitely many denominators remain nonzero and both discriminants remain positive.  Strict inequalities of continuous functions define a relative open neighborhood, so \(\mathcal U_p\) contains \(p\).  Cohort conditioning and matrix inversion are rational maps there; the positive square root is real analytic on \((0,\infty)\); and
\[
 C^\dagger=C^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}                             \tag{1}
\]
is analytic wherever \(CC^\top\) is nonsingular.  The construction of \(\Phi\) is a finite composition of these maps, sums, and products.  Thus \(\Phi\) has a real-analytic off-model extension on \(\mathcal U_p\).  Coordinates of \(z\in\mathcal U_p\) need not be nonnegative.

The derivative is computable by the following recurrence.  For a tangent direction \(h\) satisfying \(\mathbf 1^\top h=0\), put a dot over each recovered quantity.  First,
\[
 \dot q_d=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}h_s,
 \qquad
 \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}
 \frac{p_s+\varepsilon h_s}{q_d(p+\varepsilon h)}\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
 =\frac{h_s}{q_d}-\frac{p_s\dot q_d}{q_d^2}.                \tag{2}
\]
All slice derivatives are the corresponding marginal sums.  Next,
\[
 \dot M^{-1}=-M^{-1}\dot M M^{-1},
 \qquad
 \dot g=\frac{2\operatorname{tr}(K)\operatorname{tr}(\dot K)-4\dot{\det K}}{2g},              \tag{3}
\]
where
\[
 \dot{\det K}=K_{22}\dot K_{11}+K_{11}\dot K_{22}
              -K_{21}\dot K_{12}-K_{12}\dot K_{21}.       \tag{4}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 \dot\rho_{1,2}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\dot K)\mathbin{\pm}\dot g}{2},\qquad
 \dot P_1=\frac{\dot K-\dot\rho_2I_2}{g}-\frac{\dot g}{g}P_1,
 \qquad \dot P_2=-\dot P_1,                               \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot B_a[:,j]&=\dot P_jm_a+P_j\dot m_a,\\
 \dot F_y&=-B_a^{-1}\dot B_aF_y+B_a^{-1}\dot A_{ay},\\
 \dot q_{ay}&=\dot F_y\mathbf 1_3,\\
 \dot C_y[j,:]&=\{\dot F_y[j,:]-\dot q_{ay}[j]C_y[j,:]\}/q_{ay}[j].
 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{6}
\]
Writing \(C=C_a\) and \(N=(CC^\top)^{-1}\), differentiation of (1) gives
\[
 \dot C^\dagger
 =\dot C^\top N-C^\top N(\dot C C^\top+C\dot C^\top)N,   \tag{7}
\]
followed by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot W&=\dot A_{ba}C^\dagger+A_{ba}\dot C^\dagger,\\
 \dot c&=W^{-1}(\dot m_b-\dot Wc),\\
 \dot B_b&=\dot W\operatorname{diag}(c)+W\operatorname{diag}(\dot c).
 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{8}
\]
For \(y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 \dot q_{by}=-B_b^{-1}\dot B_bq_{by}+B_b^{-1}\dot A_{by}\mathbf 1_3.                         \tag{9}
\]
The active entries of \(\dot{\widehat Q}_j^d\) are supplied by (6) and (9), its exit entry is minus their sum, and its absorbing-row derivative is zero.  The active rows of \(\dot{\widehat R}_j^d\) are the corresponding rows of \(\dot C_y^d\), and its absorbing-row derivative is zero.  Finally,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \widehat s_j^d&=(\mathbf 1_2^\top B_a^d[:,j],\mathbf 1_2^\top B_b^d[:,j],0),\\
 \dot{\widehat\alpha}_j^d&=\dot{\widehat s}_j^d\mathbf 1_3,\\
 \dot{\widehat\nu}_j
 &=\dot{\widehat s}_j^1\widehat Q_j^1(\widehat R_j^1-\widehat R_j^0)
  +\widehat s_j^1\dot{\widehat Q}_j^1(\widehat R_j^1-\widehat R_j^0)\\
 &\quad+\widehat s_j^1\widehat Q_j^1(\dot{\widehat R}_j^1-\dot{\widehat R}_j^0),\\
 \dot{\widehat\eta}_j
 &=\{\dot{\widehat\nu}_j\widehat\alpha_j^1
      -\widehat\nu_j\dot{\widehat\alpha}_j^1\}/(\widehat\alpha_j^1)^2,\\
 \dot{\widehat\tau}&=\sum_{j=1}^2\dot{\widehat\nu}_j.
 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{10}
\]
Equations (2)--(10) determine \(J_{\Phi}(p)h\).  In particular, they propagate the estimated unnormalized active masses rather than treating mixture weights as fixed.

We now derive the saturated canonical gradient.  Let \(\mathcal S_0\) be the finite support stratum containing \(p\), and assume \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S_0\), which is relative interiority on that stratum.  A saturated score is exactly a function \(a:\mathcal S_0\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
 E_Pa(O)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_0}p_sa(s)=0.                 \tag{11}
\]
Conversely, because \(\mathcal S_0\) is finite, \(p_{\varepsilon,s}=p_s\{1+\varepsilon a(s)\}\) is a probability law for all sufficiently small \(|\varepsilon|\), and it has score \(a\).  Thus the tangent space is all of \(L_2^0(P)\).  Differentiability and (11) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Phi(p_\varepsilon)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
 &=J_{\Phi}(p)\sum_s p_se_sa(s)\\
 &=E_P\!\left[J_{\Phi}(p)(e_O-p)a(O)\right]
 =E_P\{G_p(O)a(O)\}.
 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{12}
\]
Also \(E_PG_p(O)=0\).  If \(H\) is any other centered gradient, the score equations imply \(E_P\{(H-G_p)a\}=0\) for every \(a\in L_2^0(P)\).  Taking each coordinate of \(H-G_p\) as \(a\) proves \(H=G_p\) almost surely.  Hence \(G_p\) is the canonical gradient, and its covariance is
\[
 E_P\{G_p(O)G_p(O)^\top\}
 =J_{\Phi}(p)\{\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\}J_{\Phi}(p)^\top
 =\Sigma(p).                                                \tag{13}
\]
Because every regular asymptotically linear estimator has a centered influence function satisfying the same score equations, (12) forces its influence component to be \(G_p\); thus (13) is the saturated information bound.

Finally, the exact multinomial identity is
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p-p)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(e_{O_i}-p),
 \qquad \widehat p-p=O_P(n^{-1/2}).                         \tag{14}
\]
Taylor expansion of the analytic map at fixed interior \(p\), \(\texttt{ass:iid-panels}\), and (14) give
\[
 \sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)\}
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_{\Phi}(p)(e_{O_i}-p)+o_P(1)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1).                     \tag{15}
\]
The empirical-cell plug-in therefore has canonical influence function \(G_p\) and attains (13).

Let \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) be the set of \(126\)-cell vectors induced by \(\mathcal P_\kappa\).  It is compact by \(\texttt{def:buffered-class}\).  Every inverse, division, eigengap, normalization, and reported variance required by the recovery algorithm appears in \(\mathfrak m(p)\) or in the variance buffer.  The population margins are at least \(2\kappa\), whereas the empirical guard uses \(\kappa\).

Analyticity, compactness, and the finite margin list give a fixed \(r>0\) such that the relative closed \(r\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) lies in the analytic domain, every algebraic guard there exceeds \(\kappa\), and every reported variance there exceeds \(\kappa\).  On that neighborhood there are finite constants
\[
 L_1=\sup_q\|J_{\Phi}(q)\|<\infty,
 \qquad L_2=\sup_q\|D^2\Phi(q)\|<\infty.                 \tag{1}
\]
The support-legality guard holds almost surely because every law in the class assigns zero probability to cells forbidden by the enlarged absorbing graph.  Direct multinomial calculation gives
\[
 E_P\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2
 =\frac{1-\|p\|_2^2}{n}\leq\frac1n.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P\{\|\widehat p-p\|_2>r\}
 \leq\frac1{nr^2}.                                         \tag{2}
\]
On the complementary event every sequential calculation is legal and every empirical margin exceeds \(\kappa\).  This proves
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P(\mathcal E_\kappa)\longrightarrow1.                           \tag{3}
\]

Taylor's formula and (1) give, on this event,
\[
 \left\|\sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)-J_{\Phi}(p)(\widehat p-p)\}\right\|
 \leq\frac{L_2}{2}\sqrt n\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2.           \tag{4}
\]
For each \(\varepsilon>0\), Markov's inequality bounds the probability that the right side exceeds \(\varepsilon\) by \(L_2/(2\varepsilon\sqrt n)\).  Combining this with (2), \(\Phi(p)=\theta\) from \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\), and
\[
 J_{\Phi}(p)\sqrt n(\widehat p-p)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)
\]
proves the asserted uniform asymptotic linear representation.  Assigning any fixed value off the guard event is asymptotically irrelevant by (3).

The empirical covariance has the exact finite-cell form
\[
 \widehat\Sigma
 =J_{\Phi}(\widehat p)
   \{\operatorname{diag}(\widehat p)-\widehat p\widehat p^\top\}
   J_{\Phi}(\widehat p)^\top.                              \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, (5) follows by expanding the empirical second moment of \(e_{O_i}-\widehat p\).  The right side is uniformly continuous on the compact neighborhood in (1).  Equations (2) and (5) imply, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 P\{\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(p)\|>\varepsilon\}\longrightarrow0.                            \tag{6}
\]
Thus each reported empirical diagonal exceeds \(\kappa\) with probability tending to one uniformly.  No full covariance inverse is used.

It remains to establish simultaneous coverage, including singular correlations.  Take an arbitrary sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_\kappa\).  Compactness yields a subsequence, not relabelled, with \(p_n\to p_\star\).  Continuity and the variance buffer give
\[
 \Sigma(p_n)\to\Sigma(p_\star),
 \qquad \sigma_{n,\ell}^2:=\Sigma_{\ell\ell}(p_n)\geq2\kappa.                               \tag{7}
\]
For \(\ell\in\mathcal L\), define
\[
 Y_{n,i,\ell}=G_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)/\sigma_{n,\ell},
 \qquad \Gamma_n=E_{P_n}(Y_{n,i}Y_{n,i}^\top).
\]
The diagonal of \(\Gamma_n\) is one.  Equations (1) and (7) make the summands uniformly bounded, and after taking a further subsequence \(\Gamma_n\to\Gamma_\star\), where \(\Gamma_\star\) may be singular.

For every fixed \(u\), centering and the third-order Taylor formula for the exponential, with a uniform remainder because the summands are bounded, yield
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\{iu^\top Y_{n,1}/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}).                \tag{8}
\]
Independence then implies
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\!\left\{iu^\top n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{n,i}\right\}
 =\left(1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2})\right)^n
 \longrightarrow\exp(-u^\top\Gamma_\star u/2).           \tag{9}
\]
Thus the studentized linear term converges to \(Z_\star\sim N(0,\Gamma_\star)\), including a singular limit.

Conditionally on the sample, the multiplier numerator is exactly Gaussian.  Coordinatewise studentization gives empirical correlation
\[
 \widehat\Gamma_{\ell k}
 =\frac{\widehat\Sigma_{\ell k}}
 {\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{\ell\ell}\widehat\Sigma_{kk}}}.  \tag{10}
\]
Equations (6)--(7) imply \(\widehat\Gamma\to\Gamma_\star\) in \(P_n\)-probability.  Applying \(\texttt{lem:gaussian-max-quantile-continuity}\) at \(u=1-\alpha\) gives
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}\longrightarrow c_\star             \tag{11}
\]
in probability, where \(c_\star\) is the unique \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\), and
\[
 P\{\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\leq c_\star\}=1-\alpha.                    \tag{12}
\]
The uniform linearization, (6), (9), and positive diagonals show that the coverage event differs by probability \(o(1)\) from
\[
 \left\{\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}
 \frac{|n^{-1/2}\sum_iG_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)|}{\sigma_{n,\ell}}
 \leq\widehat c_{1-\alpha}\right\}.
\]
Equations (11)--(12) give coverage tending to \(1-\alpha\) on the selected subsequence.  Since the original sequence was arbitrary, the contradiction-subsequence criterion yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 \left|P\{\theta_\ell\in I_{\ell,n}\text{ for every }\ell\in\mathcal L\}-(1-\alpha)\right|
 \longrightarrow0.                                         \tag{13}
\]
The theorem's displayed infimum follows.  The proof nowhere assumes a positive smallest eigenvalue of \(\Sigma(p)\) or its correlation matrix.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{5d}}\), and write \(\langle f,h\rangle_P=E_P\{f(O)h(O)\}\).  The active-frontier theorem proves that the causal target equals \(\Phi(p)\) on every constrained parametric submodel through \(P\), while the analytic-gradient theorem gives
\[
 \dot\theta_P[h]=E_P\{G_p(O)h(O)\},\qquad h\in\mathcal T_P.                                  \tag{1}
\]
The tangent space is closed by definition.  Hence its orthogonal projection exists.  Define coordinatewise
\[
 \psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}=\Pi_{\mathcal T_P}G_{p,\ell}.
\]
Since \(G_{p,\ell}-\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}\) is orthogonal to \(\mathcal T_P\),
\[
 \dot\theta_{P,\ell}[h]
 =\langle G_{p,\ell},h\rangle_P
 =\langle\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell},h\rangle_P
 \quad(h\in\mathcal T_P).                                  \tag{2}
\]
If another element of \(\mathcal T_P\) represents the same derivative, its difference from \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}\) lies in \(\mathcal T_P\) and is orthogonal to it, hence is zero.  This proves the efficient-gradient characterization and the covariance formula for \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\).

Put \(R_\ell=(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})G_{p,\ell}\).  Orthogonality gives
\[
 \Sigma_{\ell k}(p)
 =\langle\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell},\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,k}\rangle_P
  +\langle R_\ell,R_k\rangle_P.                            \tag{3}
\]
Thus, for every \(a\in\mathbb R^9\),
\[
 a^\top\{\Sigma(p)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}a
 =\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^9a_\ell R_\ell\right\|_{L_2(P)}^2
 =\|(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})a^\top G_p\|_{L_2(P)}^2.        \tag{4}
\]
This proves both positive-semidefinite dominance and the exact strictness criterion.

For the promised computation, enumerate the actual support as \(s=1,\ldots,m_P\), let \(W_P=\operatorname{diag}(p_1,\ldots,p_{m_P})\), and let the columns of a finite matrix \(S_P\) span the score space obtained by differentiating the absorbing support, two-type factorization, common-kernel, and date-\(4\) restrictions defining \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{5d}}\).  For coordinate \(\ell\), solve
\[
 \min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{k_P}}
 \sum_{s=1}^{m_P}p_s\{G_{p,\ell}(s)-S_P[s,:]\beta\}^2.     \tag{5}
\]
The normal equations and unique fitted value are
\[
 S_P^\top W_PS_P\beta=S_P^\top W_PG_{p,\ell},
 \qquad
 \psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}
 =S_P(S_P^\top W_PS_P)^\dagger S_P^\top W_PG_{p,\ell}.     \tag{6}
\]
The Moore--Penrose inverse makes the fitted value invariant to redundant score generators.

On a smooth local stratum of constant tangent rank, choose independent score coordinates \(\zeta\) for which \(I_P=S_P^\top W_PS_P\) is nonsingular.  The local likelihood score expansion is
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\zeta-\zeta)
 =I_P^{-1}n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nS_P[O_i,:]^\top+o_P(1).       \tag{7}
\]
Equation (1) gives the target derivative
\[
 \dot\theta_{\ell,\zeta}=G_{p,\ell}^\top W_PS_P.           \tag{8}
\]
Combining (7)--(8) produces exactly (6), so the corresponding local likelihood estimator, or its one-step equivalent, attains \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\) pointwise on that stratum.

The broad class \(\mathcal P_\kappa\) buffers the four-slice recovery and saturated marginal variances, but it neither imposes the date-\(4\) common-kernel restriction nor bounds the positive singular values of the constrained score information away from zero.  It also permits support and tangent-rank changes.  Therefore (1)--(8) do not imply uniform constrained efficiency over \(\mathcal P_\kappa\), and no such conclusion is asserted.

Let \(L=\operatorname{range}(\Gamma^{1/2})\).  Since every diagonal entry of \(\Gamma\) is one, \(L\neq\{0\}\), and the law of \(Z\) has a strictly positive Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(L\).  The restriction of \(x\mapsto\|x\|_\infty\) to \(L\) is a norm.  For \(0\leq s<t\), choose nonzero \(x\in L\) and rescale it so that \(s<\|x\|_\infty<t\).  The set
\[
 \{y\in L:s<\|y\|_\infty<t\}
\]
contains a nonempty relatively open subset of \(L\), and hence has strictly positive Gaussian probability.  Thus the distribution function of \(\|Z\|_\infty\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\).

For every \(t\geq0\),
\[
 \{\|Z\|_\infty=t\}\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^q\{|Z_k|=t\}.
\]
Every marginal \(Z_k\) is \(N(0,1)\), even when the joint covariance is singular, so the finite union has probability zero.  The distribution function is continuous, starts at zero, and tends to one.  Its \(u\)-quantile \(c_u(\Gamma)\) is therefore unique for every \(u\in(0,1)\).

For every \(v\in\mathbb R^q\),
\[
 E\exp(i v^\top Z_n)=\exp(-v^\top\Gamma_nv/2)
 \longrightarrow\exp(-v^\top\Gamma v/2)=E\exp(i v^\top Z).
\]
Thus \(Z_n\) converges in distribution to \(Z\), including when \(\Gamma\) is singular.  Continuity of the maximum norm implies convergence in distribution of the maxima.  If \(F_n,F\) are their distribution functions and \(c=c_u(\Gamma)\), strict increase and continuity give, for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 F(c-\varepsilon)<u<F(c+\varepsilon).
\]
Convergence at the two continuity points makes the same inequalities true for \(F_n\) for all large \(n\), whence
\[
 c-\varepsilon<c_u(\Gamma_n)<c+\varepsilon.
\]
Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves quantile convergence without a lower eigenvalue bound.

added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) and \(d\in\{0,1\}\).  By \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\), conditioning on \(D=d\) is legitimate.  For \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), define the proof intermediates
\[
 B_x[u,j]=P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d),\qquad
 D_{xy}=\operatorname{diag}\{Q_1[x,y],Q_2[x,y]\},
\]
and let
\[
 C_y[j,v]=P(X_3=v\mid X_2=y,Z=j,D=d),\qquad v\in\mathcal S.
\]
The rows of \(C_y\) are probability vectors, so \(C_y\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_2\).  Consistency and no anticipation identify the observed path through date \(2\) with either potential path.  Conditional first-order Markov factorization and the common date-\(2\) kernel then give, entry by entry,
\[
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 =\sum_{j=1}^2B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y[j,v],
 \qquad A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}C_y.                              \tag{1}
\]
This is a date-specific factorization; no equality between kernels at different dates is used.

Let \(\bar C_y=C_y[:,\mathcal A]\).  Restricting (1) to active terminal columns yields
\[
 \bar A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}\bar C_y.                           \tag{2}
\]
Every factor in (2) is \(2\times2\).  By \(\texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}\), every matrix on the left is nonsingular.  Hence the determinant identity for (2) implies that \(B_a,B_b,\bar C_a,\bar C_b\) and every \(D_{xy}\) are nonsingular.  In particular,
\[
 Q_j[x,y]>0\quad(j=1,2;\ x,y\in\mathcal A),                 \tag{3}
\]
because these entries are nonnegative probabilities, and both \(C_a\) and \(C_b\) have row rank two.

Substituting (2) into the observable cycle product and cancelling only invertible factors gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 K^d
 &=B_aD_{aa}\bar C_a(B_bD_{ba}\bar C_a)^{-1}
   B_bD_{bb}\bar C_b(B_aD_{ab}\bar C_b)^{-1}\\
 &=B_aD_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}B_a^{-1}\\
 &=B_a\operatorname{diag}(r_1,r_2)B_a^{-1},
 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{4}
\]
where
\[
 r_j=\frac{Q_j[a,a]Q_j[b,b]}{Q_j[b,a]Q_j[a,b]}>0.            \tag{5}
\]
The two eigenvalues are distinct by \(\texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum}\).  Thus the definitions of \(g^d\) and \(\rho_j^d\) order them decreasingly, and, with \(E_j\) the diagonal coordinate projector,
\[
 P_j^d=B_aE_jB_a^{-1}.                                      \tag{6}
\]

Absorption implies \(X_0=e\Rightarrow X_1=e\).  Consequently every path with \(X_1=a\) has \(X_0\in\mathcal A\), and summing over types gives
\[
 m_a^d=B_a\mathbf 1_2.
\]
Combining this equality with (6),
\[
 P_j^dm_a^d=B_aE_j\mathbf 1_2=B_a[:,j].                     \tag{7}
\]
Hence the matrix called \(B_a^d\) by the recovery map is exactly the unnormalized latent component predecessor matrix, including its scale.

Using (1), (3), and (7),
\[
 F_y^d=(B_a^d)^{-1}A_{ay}^d=D_{ay}C_y,
 \qquad q_{ay}^d=F_y^d\mathbf 1_3=D_{ay}\mathbf 1_2.        \tag{8}
\]
Therefore \(q_{ay}^d[j]=Q_j[a,y]>0\), and stochastic row-sum normalization gives
\[
 C_y^d=\operatorname{diag}(q_{ay}^d)^{-1}F_y^d=C_y.          \tag{9}
\]
The use of all three terminal columns in (8) is what recovers the normalization in the presence of exit.

Because \(C_a\) has row rank two,
\[

\]
Equations (1) and (9) imply
\[
 W^d=A_{ba}^dC_a^\dagger=B_bD_{ba}.                         \tag{10}
\]
This matrix is nonsingular.  Absorption again gives \(m_b^d=B_b\mathbf 1_2\), and hence
\[

 \qquad B_b^d=W^d\operatorname{diag}(c^d)=B_b.              \tag{11}
\]
Repeating (8) with \(x=b\) recovers \(Q_j[b,y]\) for \(y\in\mathcal A\).  Row stochasticity recovers
\[

\]

Define the recovered unnormalized active-date-\(1\) row vector by
\[

\[

Each column of the nonsingular nonnegative matrices \(B_a\) and \(B_b\) has positive sum, so \(\alpha_j^d>0\).  Thus every division by \(\alpha_j^d\) used for an at-risk conditional law is legitimate.

Equations (1), (7)--(13) recover the entire unnormalized component sublaw on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\).  For example, for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\) and \(v\in\mathcal S\), its cell mass conditional on \(D=d\) is
\[

\]

\[

\[

Conditioning on \((Z,X_1,X_2)\), using (16), therefore proves the causal rather than definitional identity
\[
 \begin{aligned}

 &=E\!\left[\mathbf 1\{Z=j\}
  \{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}
  \mid D=1\right]\\

 \end{aligned}                                               \tag{17}
\]
Here paths with \(X_1=e\) contribute zero: no anticipation gives \(X_1(1)=X_1(0)=e\), and repeated use of \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) gives \(X_3(1)=X_3(0)=e\).  Because \(\alpha_j^1>0\), division of (17) yields
\[

\]
Summing (17) over the partition \(Z=1,2\) proves
\[

At every law \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{5d}}\) at which the constrained tangent space \(\mathcal T_P\) is defined on its actual finite support, the constrained efficient influence function is the coordinatewise orthogonal projection \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}=\Pi_{\mathcal T_P}G_p\), and the constrained efficiency bound is \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)=E_P\{\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}(O)\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}(O)^\top\}\).  For every \(a\in\mathbb R^9\),
\[
 a^\top\{\Sigma(p)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}a
 =\|(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})a^\top G_p\|_{L_2(P)}^2.
\]
Thus the constrained bound is strictly smaller than the saturated bound in direction \(a\) exactly when \(a^\top G_p\notin\mathcal T_P\).  On a smooth local stratum with constant tangent rank and nonsingular information for independent score coordinates, the projection is computable from a finite score matrix by weighted least squares, and a regular local likelihood or one-step estimator attains this bound pointwise.  These conclusions do not establish uniform constrained efficiency over \(\mathcal P_{\kappa}\), which neither imposes the date-\(4\) restriction nor buffers constrained score rank or support changes.

prose_updates.tldr:
Four matched active-state slices identify the unnormalized latent-type sublaws among units active at date \(1\), even when a common absorbing state makes all-state terminal factors singular and some units are already absorbed. Spectral projectors fix scale, terminal row sums recover exit probabilities, and a full-row-rank pseudoinverse transports the second active predecessor factor. Absorption plus no anticipation makes initially absorbed units' treatment effects zero, so the type contributions \(
u_j\), at-risk effects \(
u_j/\alpha_j^1\), and aggregate ATT \(	au=\sum_j
u_j\) are point identified over the full broad fiber. The observable no-date-\(1\)-absorption subface additionally identifies full type masses and conditional type effects. The corrected analytic \(126\)-cell map has a saturated multinomial canonical gradient and guarded multiplier bands with uniform coverage under singular correlation; fifth-date constrained efficiency is stated only on a separate subclass.

project_justification.gap: Published short-panel Markov-mixture reconstruction and the adjacent transition-independence theorem use rank or positivity hypotheses that exclude a common absorbing terminal row. They also do not characterize the identification elbow created when latent types may contain units already absorbed before the active recovery cut: full conditional type effects can fail even though all aggregate causal effects remain identified.
project_justification.niche: Two active states and one absorbing exit state leave four invertible active minors. Their cycle product identifies common type signatures, stochastic row sums identify unnormalized active masses and exit transitions, and absorption converts the omitted initially absorbed subpopulation from an identification obstacle for aggregates into a zero-effect component.
project_justification.fill: The project gives an explicit projector, row-sum, and pseudoinverse map for active component sublaws, type contributions, at-risk type effects, and the aggregate ATT on the broad absorbing class; a no-initial-absorption corollary for full conditional type effects; the exact sharp-frontier witness; an analytic saturated gradient; and uniform guarded multiplier bands on the enlarged support.

sampling_model.design: Observational two-cohort panel with adoption at date \(3\) for \(D=1\), no adoption for \(D=0\), and an absorbing exit state; date-\(1\) absorption is allowed in the headline class.
sampling_model.units: \(n\) independent and identically distributed complete five-date panels \(O_i\) on the \(126\)-cell absorption-legal support.
sampling_model.treatment: Cohort membership fixes the realized treatment path; no anticipation holds through date \(2\), and units absorbed by date \(1\) have identical absorbed potential continuations.
sampling_model.overlap: Both cohorts and both latent types have positive probability; four-slice rank further implies positive active mass \(\alpha_j^d\) for each type and cohort.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No nonparametric nuisance is fitted. Empirical frequencies on the fixed \(126\)-cell support feed the guarded analytic contribution-recovery map.

prose_updates.related_work: Ahn and Kasahara (2026), Proposition 14 and Appendix A.4, provide the closest causal setup and inverse-cancellation architecture, but their published full-rank and positive-transition hypothesis class excludes the common absorbing boundary; the present result is an excluded-boundary extension, not an application of that class. Higgins and Jochmans (2023) and Gupta, Kumar, and Vassilvitskii (2016) reconstruct Markov mixtures under their respective time-homogeneity, component-rank, state-count, and nondegeneracy regimes; those scaling and label ideas are prior art, while the present theorem is a causal, time-varying active-minor result and does not subsume them. Restricted hidden-Markov measurement results likewise answer reconstruction questions under their own emission or structural restrictions, not the potential-path contribution identity proved here. Deaner and Ku (2026) motivate transition restrictions for absorbing duration outcomes but study aggregate duration difference-in-differences rather than latent-type multi-state reconstruction. Bonhomme, Jochmans, and Robin (2017) motivate differentiating diagonalization estimators; Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2013, 2015) provide neighboring Gaussian bootstrap and anti-concentration tools. Rao and Risch (2026) are the interpretation consumer: an incumbent-firm panel could use active productivity states and exit to study offsetting latent-type contributions, but this note does not claim their data satisfy its model or iid sampling assumptions.
prose_updates.interpretation:
The broad result separates three quantities that are often conflated. The full share \(\pi_j^d\) counts every member of latent type \(j\), including those already absorbed; the active share \(\alpha_j^d\) counts only members active at the recovery cut; and \(
u_j\) is the type's unnormalized contribution to the aggregate causal state shift. Active slices identify \(\alpha_j^d\), \(
u_j\), and the at-risk effect \(
u_j/\alpha_j^1\). They cannot determine which latent label owns already-absorbed zero-effect mass, so \(\pi_j^d\) and the full conditional \(	au_j\) need not be identified. If observed date-\(1\) absorption is absent, \(\alpha_j^d=\pi_j^d\), and the full conditional effects are recovered. Rao and Risch's setting is a motivation for this decomposition, not an empirical application carried out here.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The covariance \(\Sigma(p)\) is the efficiency bound for the specified off-model continuation \(\Phi\) in the saturated multinomial support-stratum model. It is not automatically the efficiency bound in the smaller fifth-date constrained Markov model. The latter uses the projected gradient only pointwise on smooth constant-rank strata, and the broad buffered class does not control constrained score rank or support changes. The exact multiplier quantile is the mathematical object; a fixed number of Monte Carlo draws needs a separate approximation error analysis. The sharp-frontier pair changes full latent type shares and full conditional type effects while preserving active shares, at-risk effects, both contribution vectors, and the entire aggregate ATT vector.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The proposal proves a sufficient constructive frontier for two known latent types, two active states, one absorbing exit, four nonsingular matched active slices, simple common cycle signatures, cohort and type overlap, type-conditional first-order Markov potential paths, no anticipation, and common untreated date-\(2\) and first-post kernels. It does not establish necessity beyond the explicit initial-absorption pair, identify unknown type count, handle weak eigengaps, justify clustered policy-panel inference, or allow approximate common transitions. Full conditional type effects require the observable no-date-\(1\)-absorption subface; the broad class identifies active sublaws, type contributions, at-risk effects, and the aggregate. Date-\(4\) common-kernel information is used only in the separately named constrained-efficiency subclass.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write all state vectors in the order \((a,b,e)\).  We first construct the full-data law promised by \(\texttt{def:exact-witness}\), so that consistency and the cross-world claims are checked rather than inferred from an observed factorization.  Put \(R_{j,0}=Q_j\) and \(R_{j,1}=V_j\).  For \(d,r\in\{0,1\}\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), \(s_0\in\mathcal A\), and states \(s_1,s_2,u_0,w_0,u_1,w_1\in\mathcal S\), assign joint mass
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P\{D=d,Z=j,X_0(0)=X_0(1)=s_0,
X_1(0)=X_1(1)=s_1,X_2(0)=X_2(1)=s_2,\\
&\hspace{42mm}X_3(0)=u_0,X_4(0)=w_0,
X_3(1)=u_1,X_4(1)=w_1\}\\
&\quad =\frac18 H_j[s_0,s_1]Q_j[s_1,s_2]
Q_j[s_2,u_0]Q_j[u_0,w_0]
V_j[s_2,u_1]V_j[u_1,w_1].
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{1}
\]
All other configurations receive mass zero.  Every displayed matrix in \(\texttt{def:exact-witness}\) has nonnegative entries and obeys
\[
H_j\mathbf 1_3=Q_j\mathbf 1_3=V_j\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3,
\quad H_j[e,{:}]=Q_j[e,{:}]=V_j[e,{:}]=(0,0,1).              \tag{2}
\]
Successive summation of (1), using (2), gives total mass one.  Define the observed process by \(X_t=X_t(D)\).  This gives \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\), while the three shared coordinates through date \(2\) give \(\texttt{ass:no-anticipation}\).  Marginalizing from (1) the continuation belonging to the other path gives, conditional on \((D,Z)\), transition sequence \((H_j,Q_j,Q_j,Q_j)\) for \(r=0\) and \((H_j,Q_j,V_j,V_j)\) for \(r=1\).  Thus \(\texttt{ass:markov-paths}\) holds.  Equation (2) proves support on \(\mathcal G\) and \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\).  Moreover,
\[
P(D=d)=\frac12,\quad P(Z=j\mid D=d)=\frac12,                \tag{3}
\]
so \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\), \(\texttt{ass:type-overlap}\), and \(\texttt{ass:two-types}\) hold.  Taking the date-\(2\) common kernel to be \(Q_j\) and the untreated first-post kernel to be \(U_j=Q_j\) verifies \(\texttt{ass:common-date-two-transition}\) and \(\texttt{ass:common-first-post-untreated-transition}\).  No common date-\(4\) restriction is needed.  Finally, \(X_0\in\mathcal A\) almost surely and the active rows of \(H_j\) have zero exit probability, so
\[
P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0.                                          \tag{4}
\]
In particular, the witness satisfies the additional condition \(\texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}\).

We next verify the rank and spectral requirements in the definition of \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).  For \(x\in\mathcal A\), define the component predecessor matrix
\[
B_x[u,j]=P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d)=\frac14H_j[u,x].          \tag{5}
\]
It is independent of \(d\), and direct substitution gives
\[
B_a=\begin{pmatrix}3/16&1/12\\1/16&1/6\end{pmatrix},\quad
B_b=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/6\\3/16&1/12\end{pmatrix},
\quad \det(B_a)=\frac5{192},\quad \det(B_b)=-\frac5{192}. \tag{6}
\]
Let \(D_{xy}=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1[x,y],Q_2[x,y])\).  Let row \(j\) of \(C_y^0\) be row \(y\) of \(Q_j\), and let row \(j\) of \(C_y^1\) be row \(y\) of \(V_j\).  The Markov factorization of (1) gives, entry by entry,
\[
A_{xy}^d[u,v]=\sum_{j=1}^2B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v],
\quad A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}C_y^d.                              \tag{7}
\]
For the active terminal minors \(\bar C_y^d=C_y^d[:,\mathcal A]\), exact calculation yields
\[
\det(\bar C_a^0)=\frac9{50},\quad
\det(\bar C_b^0)=-\frac3{100},\quad
\det(\bar C_a^1)=\frac{31}{100},\quad
\det(\bar C_b^1)=-\frac1{20}.                               \tag{8}
\]
Since
\[
\det(\bar A_{xy}^d)=\det(B_x)Q_1[x,y]Q_2[x,y]\det(\bar C_y^d), \tag{9}
\]
equations (6)--(8) give, in the order \((aa,ab,ba,bb)\),
\[
\left(\det\bar A_{aa}^0,\det\bar A_{ab}^0,
\det\bar A_{ba}^0,\det\bar A_{bb}^0\right)
=\left(\frac9{16000},-\frac3{32000},-\frac9{32000},\frac3{12800}\right), \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
\left(\det\bar A_{aa}^1,\det\bar A_{ab}^1,
\det\bar A_{ba}^1,\det\bar A_{bb}^1\right)
=\left(\frac{31}{32000},-\frac1{6400},-\frac{31}{64000},\frac1{2560}\right). \tag{11}
\]
All eight determinants are nonzero.  Therefore every active slice is nonsingular; because there are finitely many, the minimum of their positive smallest singular values is positive.  This proves \(\texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}\).

Restricting (7) to active terminal columns and substituting into the cycle product cancels all adjacent terminal and predecessor factors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
K^d
&=B_aD_{aa}\bar C_a^d(B_bD_{ba}\bar C_a^d)^{-1}
B_bD_{bb}\bar C_b^d(B_aD_{ab}\bar C_b^d)^{-1}\\
&=B_aD_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}B_a^{-1}.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{12}
\]
Every inverse and division in (12) is legitimate by (6), (8), and the strictly positive active entries of \(Q_1,Q_2\).  The middle factor is
\[
D_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}
=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
\frac{(3/5)(1/2)}{(1/5)(3/10)},
\frac{(1/5)(3/5)}{(3/10)(2/5)}\right)
=\operatorname{diag}(5,1).                                  \tag{13}
\]
Since \(B_a=48^{-1}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}9&4\\3&8\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), equations (12)--(13) imply
\[
K^d=\frac1{60}
\begin{pmatrix}45&4\\15&8\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}8&-4\\-3&9\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}.          \tag{14}
\]
Its trace is \(6\) and its determinant is \(5\), hence
\[
\det(\lambda I_2-K^d)=\lambda^2-6\lambda+5=(\lambda-5)(\lambda-1),
\quad g^d=\sqrt{6^2-4\cdot5}=4>0.                          \tag{15}
\]
This proves the ordered spectrum and \(\texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum}\).  Equations (2)--(4), (10)--(11), and (15), together with the preceding structural checks, establish \(\omega^\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).

We now calculate causal contrasts directly from the potential-path law.  The uniform active initial law is invariant under both \(H_1\) and \(H_2\).  Consequently, the type-specific date-\(2\) laws in the treated cohort are
\[
p_{2,1}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_1Q_1=(2/5,2/5,1/5),
\quad
p_{2,2}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_2Q_2=(1/4,1/2,1/4).                  \tag{16}
\]
The two paths share \(X_2\) in (1).  Conditional on \((X_2,Z,D=1)\), their date-\(3\) kernels are \(V_j\) and \(Q_j\), respectively.  The definition of \(\tau_j\) and iterated expectation therefore give
\[
\tau_j=p_{2,j}^1(V_j-Q_j).                                  \tag{17}
\]
The two exact products are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_1
&=(2/5,2/5,1/5)
\begin{pmatrix}1/10&-1/10&0\\0&1/10&-1/10\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
=(1/25,0,-1/25),\\
\tau_2
&=(1/4,1/2,1/4)
\begin{pmatrix}0&1/10&-1/10\\-1/20&-1/10&3/20\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20).
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{18}
\]
By (3), total expectation over \(Z\) gives
\[
\tau=\frac12\tau_1+\frac12\tau_2=(3/400,-1/80,1/200).      \tag{19}
\]
Equation (4) implies \(\alpha_j^d=P(Z=j\mid D=d)=1/2\).  Since there are no initially absorbed units under \(\omega^\star\), the causal definition of the unnormalized contribution gives
\[
\nu_j=P(Z=j\mid D=1)\tau_j=\frac12\tau_j.                  \tag{20}
\]
Substitution from (18) yields
\[
\nu_1=(1/50,0,-1/50),\quad
\nu_2=(-1/80,-1/80,1/40).                                   \tag{21}
\]
Conditioning additionally on \(X_1\in\mathcal A\) changes nothing under (4), so \(\eta_j=\tau_j\).

We turn to the pair in \(\texttt{def:outside-face-pair}\).  On its added component, set \(X_t(0)=X_t(1)=e\) at every date.  For either cohort and \(C\in\{A,B\}\), marginalizing the latent label gives
\[
P^C(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
=\frac45P_{\omega^\star}(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
+\frac15\mathbf 1\{x_{0:4}=(e,e,e,e,e)\}.                  \tag{22}
\]
Because the cohort law is unchanged, (22) proves equality of the complete observed laws of \(P^A\) and \(P^B\), not merely equality of selected moments.

Both laws satisfy every condition defining the broad class.  Consistency and no anticipation hold separately on both mixture components.  Conditional on \((D,Z)\), at an active current state the posterior probability of the all-exit component is zero, so the next-state row is the corresponding row of the original kernel; at current state \(e\), both components move to \(e\) with probability one by (2).  Hence each marginal potential path remains first-order Markov, absorption remains valid, and the common date-\(2\) and untreated first-post kernels remain \(Q_j\).  Cohort overlap is unchanged.  Each type retains active mass \((4/5)(1/2)=2/5\), so both type shares are positive.  Finally, the all-exit component enters none of the events indexing an active slice.  Thus
\[
A_{xy}^{C,d}=\frac45A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d},\quad
\bar A_{xy}^{C,d}=\frac45\bar A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d},
\quad x,y\in\mathcal A.                                   \tag{23}
\]
The nonzero determinants in (10)--(11) remain nonzero, proving the slice-rank condition for both laws.  In the four-factor cycle product, the scalar multipliers cancel:
\[
(4/5)(4/5)^{-1}(4/5)(4/5)^{-1}=1.                           \tag{24}
\]
Therefore both cycle products equal (14), and both laws have the same simple ordered signature \(5>1\).  This common signature also fixes the same type labels in the two laws.  We have proved \(P^A,P^B\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).  Their added component also gives
\[
P^A(X_1=e\mid D=d)=P^B(X_1=e\mid D=d)=\frac15,              \tag{25}
\]
so neither law satisfies the additional no-date-\(1\)-absorption restriction.

The active component contributes \(2/5\) to each type in each cohort.  Allocating the additional \(1/5\) to type \(1\) under \(P^A\) and to type \(2\) under \(P^B\) gives
\[
(\pi_1^{A,d},\pi_2^{A,d})=(3/5,2/5),\quad
(\pi_1^{B,d},\pi_2^{B,d})=(2/5,3/5),                        \tag{26}
\]
whereas in both laws
\[
\alpha_1^d=\alpha_2^d=\frac25.                              \tag{27}
\]
To separate the causal numerator from these full type masses, define
\[
\Delta=\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0)).
\]
On \(\{D=1,X_1=e\}\), consistency gives \(X_1(1)=e\), no anticipation gives \(X_1(0)=X_1(1)=e\), and absorption applied separately to both potential paths gives \(X_3(0)=X_3(1)=e\).  Hence
\[
\Delta=0\quad\text{on }\{D=1,X_1=e\}.                      \tag{28}
\]
The added all-exit component therefore contributes zero.  The retained \(\omega^\star\) component contributes \((4/5)(1/2)\tau_j^{\omega^\star}\), so for both \(C=A,B\),
\[
\nu_j^C=E_C\{\mathbf 1(Z=j)\Delta\mid D=1\}
=\frac25\tau_j^{\omega^\star}.                             \tag{29}
\]
Using (18), equation (29) becomes
\[
\nu_1^A=\nu_1^B=(2/125,0,-2/125),\quad
\nu_2^A=\nu_2^B=(-1/100,-1/100,1/50).                       \tag{30}
\]
Because the masses in (27) are positive, division is legitimate.  Equations (28)--(29) and the definition of the at-risk effect give
\[
\eta_j^C=E_C(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)

For the full conditional effects, (28) and total expectation within type imply
\[
\tau_j^C=E_C(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j)=\frac{\nu_j^C}{\pi_j^{C,1}}. \tag{32}
\]
All denominators in (32) are positive by (26).  Combining (26), (30), and (32) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_1^A&=(2/75,0,-2/75),&
\tau_2^A&=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20),\\
\tau_1^B&=(1/25,0,-1/25),&
\tau_2^B&=(-1/60,-1/60,1/30).
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{33}
\]

\[

=(3/500,-1/100,1/250),\quad C=A,B.                          \tag{34}
\]
This proves equality of the entire aggregate vector, rather than only its exit coordinate.

Hence the additional support restriction removes exactly the initial-absorber allocation ambiguity exhibited by the pair.
